title: Quantum Multiscale Modeling: A Hierarchy of Algorithms for Complex Chemical Systems
authors: Seenivasan Hariharan, Kareljan Schoutens, Sachin Kinge, Lucas Visscher
abstract: Multiscale modeling of complex chemical systems requires algorithms that operate coherently across electronic, atomistic, mesoscopic, and continuum scales. While quantum algorithms have been proposed for each regime, no systematic framework exists to compose them across scale boundaries. Here, we identify the conditions under which fault-tolerant quantum algorithms might preserve scale-specific quantum advantages. We map quantum phase estimation, Hamiltonian simulation with Gibbs state preparation, quantum random walks, and quantum partial differential equation solvers onto electronic structure, molecular dynamics, mesoscopic kinetics, and continuum reactor physics, respectively. Crucially, these correspondences do not imply unconditional end-to-end quantum advantage; speedups depend heavily on state preparation, memory architectures, matrix conditioning, and classical readout costs. Six unresolved questions define this composition problem, illustrated via a quantum hierarchy for \ce{CO} oxidation over \ce{Pt(111)}. We propose viewing inter-scale transfer as a quantum channel composition problem at the interface of algorithm design and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, and ask whether information loss at scale boundaries is intrinsic to multiscale modeling or merely a consequence of lossy classical transduction between algorithmic layers. The resulting roadmap suggests that multiscale quantum advantage is governed primarily by the structure of information transfer between algorithmic layers, rather than by performance at individual scales alone.
summary: This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework for achieving end-to-end quantum advantage in multiscale simulations of complex chemistry. It moves beyond merely applying quantum algorithms to individual physical regimes by rigorously analyzing the inter-scale information transfer as a composition of quantum channels. The central argument is that the fidelity of this boundary communication dictates whether a true, scalable quantum speedup can be realized.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a systematic, coherent quantum framework for multiscale modeling that can maintain quantum advantage across disparate physical scales (electronic to continuum). The authors aim to treat inter-scale information transfer as a composition of quantum channels.
main_result: End-to-end quantum advantage depends critically on the structure and fidelity of the information transfer between algorithmic layers, rather than solely on achieving speedups at individual physical scales. They propose viewing this interface as a quantum channel composition problem.
method: The work maps established classical multiscale techniques (e.g., DFT $ightarrow$ MD $ightarrow$ kMC $ightarrow$ PDEs) onto corresponding fault-tolerant quantum algorithms (QPE, Hamiltonian simulation, QRW, QSVT solvers). The core methodology involves analyzing the information flow across these boundaries as composed quantum channels.
model_or_system: The framework is demonstrated using complex chemical systems, specifically CO oxidation over Pt(111), which requires coupling four distinct physical scales: electronic ($\sim 1$ Å), atomistic ($\sim 10$ nm), mesoscopic ($\sim 1 \mu$m), and continuum ($\sim 1$ cm).
key_observables: Conversion, selectivity, operando stability, adsorption energies ($\Delta E_{	ext{ads}}$), activation barriers ($E_a$), turnover frequency (TOF), and the propagation of quantum measurement uncertainty.
important_parameters: The scales themselves define key parameters: time/length separation (fs to s), temperature dependence ($T$), coverage ($	heta$), and algorithmic constraints like memory architecture and matrix conditioning.
main_assumptions: It is assumed that fault-tolerant quantum algorithms exist for each scale, but the primary focus shifts to characterizing the information loss or preservation during the transition between these layers. The authors highlight several unresolved questions regarding complexity bounds and error propagation.
figures_summary: The notes suggest a hierarchical structure (Table 1) mapping physical scales to classical methods and their quantum analogues, emphasizing the proposed 'quantum channel' for inter-scale transfer.
paper_structure: The paper systematically identifies the four necessary physical scales, maps canonical algorithms onto them, and then focuses heavily on developing the mathematical formalism to treat the information passing *between* these layers as a composed quantum map, culminating in defining key open questions regarding uncertainty propagation and total query complexity.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum computation theory with complex condensed matter/surface science modeling. For AMO physicists, it suggests that future breakthroughs in simulating large chemical systems might require treating the entire simulation pipeline—not just the core Hamiltonian evolution—as a quantum information problem.
